title: Mapping the Old Trees
passage:
Our forest survey takes place on Saturday. Volunteers will record the locations of old trees on sheets supplied at the meeting point. Please read the route notes emailed to you before you arrive. The notes explain which entrance to use and where to meet.

The route includes uneven ground, so everyone must arrive wearing strong shoes. There is also an online group where you can introduce yourself to other volunteers beforehand. Joining it is optional; all essential information will be sent by email.

Please bring a filled water bottle, as drinking water is not available along the route. After the survey, you will upload your completed records from home. The organisers will combine these records into a map, which volunteers can view online when it is finished.

title: Looking After Drawings
passage:
Protecting a museum drawing involves more than repairing visible damage. Light can harm both paper and the materials used to make an image, even before a visitor notices a change. Museums therefore keep sensitive drawings under low lighting and limit the length of their exhibitions.

Other conservation work addresses different problems. A conservator may remove harmful dirt from a drawing's surface or repair a tear in the paper. Photographs and written records document the object's condition before treatment. Such work is valuable, but it does not replace controls on light exposure.

Between exhibitions, sensitive drawings return to storage away from display lighting. This reduces further exposure rather than reversing damage already caused. By rotating the works on their walls, museums can offer visitors changing exhibitions while giving individual drawings periods out of the light.
topic: Methods used to reduce light exposure for drawings
option1: Repairing tears in drawings before returning them to exhibitions.
option2: Keeping sensitive drawings under carefully controlled low lighting levels.
option3: Removing harmful surface dirt from drawings during conservation treatment.
option4: Limiting the time individual drawings remain on public display.
option5: Recording the condition of individual drawings through detailed photographs.
option6: Returning sensitive drawings to storage between their exhibition periods.
explanation:
Keeping sensitive drawings under carefully controlled low lighting levels.
Evidence: "Museums therefore keep sensitive drawings under low lighting"

Limiting the time individual drawings remain on public display.
Evidence: "limit the length of their exhibitions"

Returning sensitive drawings to storage between their exhibition periods.
Evidence: "Between exhibitions, sensitive drawings return to storage away from display lighting."

title: My First Kitchen Project
passage:
When I joined the community kitchen, I could follow a recipe but had never cooked for a large group. During the project, I learned to calculate how much food we needed from the number of guests. The organiser then taught me to share jobs according to each volunteer's experience, rather than giving everyone the same task.

At first, I found it difficult to explain a recipe without doing everything myself. By the final session, I could give clear instructions to newer volunteers and let them complete the work.

There were other benefits too. I met neighbours I had never spoken to before. After our last event, we were allowed to take home the food left over. Everyone who completed the project also received a certificate, which I keep beside a photograph of our kitchen team.

title: Ideas on the Move
passage:
In a 2014 study, researchers investigated whether walking affected different kinds of thinking. Adults completed tasks while sitting or walking. One involved suggesting unusual but possible uses for everyday objects. Another required finding a single word linking three other words.

Walking improved performance on the creative uses task, but did not improve performance on the task with one correct answer. Some participants also showed a creative benefit when they sat down shortly after walking. The effect was therefore not restricted to moments when their feet were moving.

Outdoor scenery was not essential: participants walking on an indoor treadmill, facing a blank wall, also benefited creatively. The research supports using a walk to help generate ideas. It does not show that walking improves every kind of thinking or every stage of a creative project.

option2: Walking improved accuracy on tasks requiring single correct answers.
option3: Indoor walking also improved participants' performance on creative tasks.
option4: Creative benefits sometimes remained after participants sat down again.
option5: Outdoor scenery was necessary for improvements in creative performance.
option6: Creative benefits disappeared immediately when participants stopped physically walking.
explanation:
Walking helped adults produce original ideas for everyday objects.
Evidence: "Walking improved performance on the creative uses task"

Indoor walking also improved participants' performance on creative tasks.

Evidence: "Some participants also showed a creative benefit when they sat down shortly after walking."

title: A Place to Begin
passage:
An arts centre that removes entrance fees may attract more visitors without making it easier for beginners to take part. Watching an exhibition and risking a first attempt at drawing are different experiences. A programme can be publicly available yet still assume that everyone arrives with equipment, confidence and spare time.

I would therefore reserve one evening each week for beginners, with materials provided and no requirement to display finished work. Regular workshops could continue on other evenings. This would extend the programme rather than replace it.

An annual exhibition would still be selected on artistic quality. Places in the beginner sessions, however, would be allocated by application order, not by portfolios. These arrangements serve different purposes: the exhibition presents accomplished work; the sessions give inexperienced people somewhere to start. Attendance figures alone would not tell us whether that second purpose had been achieved.

option3: Allocating places according to when applications are received.

title: The Blue Bottle Top
passage:
On the floor of an Australian forest, two low walls of sticks form a narrow path. A male satin bowerbird built them. The path is called a bower. A blue bottle top near its entrance might look like a piece of rubbish, but the bird chose it.

Before a female comes to look, the male collects bright blue things and arranges them around his bower. A feather or a flower will do. Near houses, he can sometimes find a blue clothes peg. When a female arrives, he bows and spreads his wings. Sometimes he dances with one of his treasures in his beak.

Where will the eggs go? The female builds a separate nest in a tree or bush and looks after the chicks on her own. The male keeps his bower ready for his next visitor.

title: When Is a Swarm Ready to Move?
passage:
A swarm of honeybees hanging from a branch may look as if it is resting. Meanwhile, a small number of bees, the scouts, are out looking for a new home. When a scout comes back, she dances on the branch. A better site gets a longer dance, which draws more scouts out to inspect it for themselves.

Researchers offered swarms two good nest boxes. When about fifteen scouts had gathered at one box, the swarm began to prepare for flight. Back on the branch, some bees were still dancing for the other box. The decision could go ahead while those bees still favoured a different home.

In another experiment, the researchers put five equally good boxes close together. Visitors spread out among them, so it took longer for a group to build up at any one box. With five homes on offer, the swarm actually left later than when there was just one.

title: Ten Metres on Six Legs
passage:
How do you tell where an ant expects its nest to be? Give it a homeward track with no nest entrance and watch where it starts doubling back. Researchers used this approach with desert ants trained to collect food ten metres from home. The centre of each ant’s search gave the team a measure of how far it believed it had travelled.

On the first outward trip, all the ants walked on legs of their usual length. At the feeder, the researchers fitted some with tiny bristles that acted as stilts and shortened the legs of others. On the return trip, the ants taking longer steps centred their searches beyond the ten-metre mark. Those taking shorter steps searched well short of it.

The timing of the change proved crucial. On later trips, the same ants walked to the feeder and back on their altered legs. Their searches clustered close to the ten-metre mark, much like those of ants whose legs had never been altered. The earlier errors had largely disappeared, even though the legs themselves had not been restored to their original length.

The findings support the idea that an ant gauges distance using its strides. Calling this a step counter is convenient shorthand. The experiment revealed how a change in stride displaced the search. It could not establish that the ant assigns a number to each step.
topic: Conclusions supported by the ants’ searches for their nest
option1: The first change in stride caused both groups to underestimate how far they needed to walk.
option2: The direction of the first error depended on whether the return stride had grown or shrunk.
option3: The usual search distance returned only once the ants had regained their original leg length.
option4: The searches established that the ants kept a numerical tally of their steps.
option5: A change in leg length caused little error when it applied to the entire round trip.
option6: The search pattern supports the idea that desert ants use information from their steps to gauge distance.
explanation:
The direction of the first error depended on whether the return stride had grown or shrunk.
Evidence: “the ants taking longer steps centred their searches beyond the ten-metre mark. Those taking shorter steps searched well short of it.”

A change in leg length caused little error when it applied to the entire round trip.
Evidence: “On later trips, the same ants walked to the feeder and back on their altered legs. Their searches clustered close to the ten-metre mark, much like those of ants whose legs had never been altered.”

The search pattern supports the idea that desert ants use information from their steps to gauge distance.

title: A Book Made with Sunlight

title: Six Places for Dots

Our guide, Rosa, had just heard from another guide on the mountain. Up there, it was hard to see even the next bend in the path. Waiting for the cloud to lift might take most of the day. Rosa took us along a lower path beside a stream instead. From time to time, we could hear water running under the stones before we could see it.

We reached an old mill just as the rain started. The picnic on the open hill was off. Rosa asked the mill owner if we could eat inside, and we spread our lunch on a long wooden table. Above us hung an old photograph of the lake on a clear day.

The lower path ended in a different village from the one on our booking. During lunch, Rosa rang the driver and arranged for him to meet us outside the village shop. The time stayed the same. Even lying down, she could see waves breaking on the rocks.

We had arrived with a bag of food and a plan to cook outside. The woman who gave us the key pointed out a small kitchen for guests. Because of the dry grass, everyone had to cook indoors. We made soup on the cooker and carried our bowls outside to eat. A cold wind soon sent us back in for our coats.

Our booking also included a visit to the tower. I thought we could choose any time to climb it, so I suggested going up after dark. The keeper explained that guests could go upstairs only with him, and that our visit was at seven the next morning. I set the alarm before we went to bed.

When it rang, neither of us wanted to move. Still, we pulled on our coats and met him at the door. From the top, we could see the roof of our little house. My sister pointed out the window where she had watched the waves from her pillow.

title: The Name on the Last Screen
passage:
Our film about the school kitchen lasted three minutes. I had filmed the cooks at work, and my friend Amir had recorded the sound. When people watched the cook cut an onion, they could hear every little tap of the knife. Amir had spent a whole lunch break getting that short piece of sound right.

The film was already on the school website when Amir noticed a problem. The last screen showed my name on its own. I had used an old list from before he joined the project. There was a class show that afternoon, and I thought about thanking him in front of everyone. Before I said anything in public, though, I went to find him. In the empty music room, I asked what he wanted me to change. He wanted people to know which part of the film he had made.

There was time to change the last screen before the show. I put Amir’s name beside the words “Sound recorded by”. At the end, two students asked him how he had made the knife sound so clear. He showed them the small microphone he had borrowed.

Later that day, I sent the corrected film to our teacher. I asked her to replace the old copy on the website, and she did. That mattered to Amir because his grandparents lived too far away to come to the show. When they watched the film that evening, his name was there.

title: Changing Sides
passage:
I nearly stopped going to chess club because of my best friend. Every Tuesday, Hugo beat me in about ten minutes. After each game, he explained so many moves that I forgot the first one before he had finished the last. I enjoyed his company. I just hated looking at the board and knowing how the afternoon would end before I had even touched a piece.

One Tuesday, Hugo brought a picture of a game that was already half finished. One player had lost several pieces and was in trouble. We set up the board to match the picture. Hugo took the weaker side for himself. For once, I had time to think about how to win, rather than how to stay in the game.

I won quite soon and reached for my bag. Hugo put all the pieces back exactly where they had been at the start of our game. This time we changed sides. I now had the difficult job he had just tried. I managed to last longer than I expected because I remembered one of his moves.

Afterwards, we each chose one move to talk about. That was our whole discussion. I could remember both ideas as I walked home. Next Tuesday, it was my turn to bring a picture, and I knew just the sort of game I wanted us to try.

title: Books in the Saddlebags
passage:
For a family living in the mountains of eastern Kentucky in the 1930s, the nearest library might as well have been in another state. A short distance on a map could mean a long journey on a poor road. The Pack Horse Library project changed who had to make that journey. A rider loaded books into bags on a horse or mule and took them out to mountain homes. Schools were stops on the riders’ routes too.

The books came from a surprising number of places. The project asked people to send books and magazines they could give away. Gifts arrived from across the United States. One man who had moved from Kentucky to California sent five hundred books in memory of his mother. Those books could keep travelling long after their first visit to a family.

With so many readers, some books soon began to fall apart. The librarians repaired what they could. Even when a book was too badly damaged to lend again, a story or picture inside it might still be easy to read. They cut out the useful parts and put them together in new books. They also made collections of recipes that people could borrow. So a rider might set out with a book that had crossed half the country and come back for another that the librarians had made themselves.

title: Taking a Temple Apart
passage:
Look at a photograph of Abu Simbel in Egypt and the seated figures outside the Great Temple seem to belong to the mountain. In a sense, they do. Long ago, workers cut the temples directly into solid rock. Yet the hillside in a photograph taken today is a different one from the hillside in an old photograph. In the 1960s, both temples moved.

A new dam was going to create a lake that would cover the old site. A wall helped keep water away while people worked, but the wall was only a temporary measure. The plan was to rebuild the temples on higher ground, beyond the reach of the rising lake.

Moving a building usually begins with finding a way to lift it. At Abu Simbel, there was no separate building to lift. Workers had to cut the original stone into more than a thousand large blocks. Each block received a number so that the team could put it back in the correct place. A piece from a face, for example, had to meet exactly the right piece on either side.

The team built a new hillside around the temples. Although the height of the site had changed, the entrances faced the same direction as before. In 1968, visitors could once again stand at the foot of the great figures. The stone above them was ancient, even though the hill supporting it was new.

title: A Record for a Stranger
passage:
Suppose somebody finds a record but has never seen a record player. How will they know where the music begins? In 1977, the people preparing two American spacecraft had to think about that question. Each Voyager spacecraft carried a round record with a gold surface. On it were sounds from Earth, including thunder, birds and people saying hello in fifty-five languages. It also carried pictures in the form of signals.

The team could hardly expect a finder in space to own the right needle to play the record. They sent one along with it. A drawing on the cover showed the needle touching the outside edge of the record. From there it was meant to move in towards the centre. A finder who started in the middle would be starting at the wrong end.

The pictures presented another problem. Even if someone found a way to turn the signals into a picture, how could they check that they had done it correctly? The first picture on the record was a circle. The team put a matching circle on the cover. If the picture a finder produced looked like a long, thin egg, they would know that its shape needed fixing.

We can understand the purpose of these little details without knowing whether anybody will ever use them. Before a distant listener could hear a single greeting, they would have to work out what the round object was for.

title: One River, Two Colours
passage:
East of the Brazilian city of Manaus, a boat can cross a line that looks almost as clear as the edge of a road. On one side, the water is pale brown. On the other, it is so dark that it looks like strong tea. There is no strip of land between the two colours. The boat is crossing from one kind of river water into another.

The pale water has travelled down the Solimões River from the direction of the Andes mountains. It carries tiny pieces of soil and rock that give it its cloudy colour. The dark water arrives in the Rio Negro. It carries very little of that material. Its colour comes mainly from old leaves and other plants breaking down on the forest floor. Water picks up colour from them on its journey to the river.

When the two rivers meet, both waters continue along the same wide channel. The pale water is cooler and moves faster than the dark water. These differences help explain why the two colours can still be seen side by side several kilometres beyond the meeting point.

If you followed the boat far enough downstream, the clear line would disappear. The moving water turns in circles in places and slowly mixes the two colours together. A photograph taken where the rivers first meet shows one stage of that journey.

title: Water from a Passing Cloud
passage:
A fishing village can have the sea on its doorstep and still have very little fresh water. In Chungungo, on the coast of Chile, water used to arrive by truck. Yet in the hills above the village, fog often passed over a high ridge. Fog contains tiny drops of water. In the early 1990s, a project began sending some of that water down to the village.

Up on the ridge, workers stretched large nets between posts. The nets stood across the path of the wind, so that the moving fog had to pass through them. A net could collect water on a day when no rain fell. As the fog passed through its small holes, little drops of water stayed behind on the thin strips of material.

One drop alone was too small to do much. Several drops joined together, grew heavier and ran down to the bottom of the net. There, a long narrow channel caught the water. A pipe carried it from the hill to the village, about seven kilometres away. People could turn on a tap at home to get water collected high above them.

The system worked for about ten years. It depended on the weather as well as on people repairing the nets. During periods without fog, the supply in the storage tank fell. A net is useful for catching water that is already in the air. An empty blue sky gives it very little to catch.

title: Is Greenland Really That Big?
passage:
Put a finger on Greenland on a Mercator world map, then find South America. Which one looks larger? On this map, Greenland can look bigger than the whole of South America. Now make the same comparison on a globe, a round model of Earth. South America covers roughly eight times the area of Greenland. How can two pictures of the same planet give such different impressions?

The difficulty begins when a mapmaker tries to show a round surface on a flat sheet. Imagine peeling an orange and pressing the skin flat without tearing or stretching it. A world map has a similar problem. Something has to change. On a Mercator map, places are stretched more as you move away from the equator towards either pole. Greenland lies far to the north, so it appears especially large.

There was a good reason for drawing the map this way. A sailor could draw a straight line between two ports and read the compass direction to follow. By keeping that direction, the sailor could follow the line. This was useful even though the line was not usually the shortest route across the sea.

For a class comparing the area of different places, a globe or a flat map that keeps areas in the correct proportion is a better choice. The sailor and the class are asking different questions, so they need different things from a map.

option3: A straight course on this map is usually the shortest route at sea.
option4: A straight line can guide a sailor who keeps one compass direction.
option5: The map shows correctly that Greenland covers more land than South America.
option6: A globe or a map that preserves area is better for comparing land sizes.

title: The Island Without a Timetable

The island looked close enough to reach before breakfast. From the harbour, a strip of pale sand appeared to join it to the mainland, and several visitors set off across it. Leila, who had come to sketch the abandoned signal station, was tempted to follow. A notice beside the quay, however, explained that the sand was exposed for only a short interval around low tide. She checked the tide board and decided to use the morning passenger boat instead of treating the sand as a reliable path.

That decision unsettled her carefully planned day. The boat would not leave for another hour, while the last return sailing depended on the weather. Leila asked the harbour officer about the forecast and wrote down the time at which passengers had to report back. When she finally reached the island, she took the inland path to the station. The exposed western track promised wider sea views, but the officer had warned that its loose stones were especially awkward in a strong wind. At the station, she spent longer drawing the machinery than she had expected. There was a great deal to notice: rust on the winch, the narrow window through which signals had once been watched, and grass growing through the floor.

By mid-afternoon the wind had risen. A few visitors suggested staying until sunset for photographs, yet Leila put away her pencils and returned to the landing stage in good time. The crew brought the sailing forward, and the boat left while there was still daylight. On the mainland, she realised that her sketch contained fewer dramatic views than she had imagined. It also contained observations she would have missed if she had rushed across the sand, struggled along the western track or waited for the last possible departure.

title: The Road Beyond the Station
passage:
When Arun booked his trip through the mountain valley, the railway was the point of it. Its small train climbed past orchards to a village where he intended to spend two nights photographing old bridges. The morning he arrived at the lower station, a landslip had closed the upper section of line. The notice offered refunds, but no estimate for reopening. Several passengers immediately searched for a private car; Arun decided that the expense would swallow most of his budget.

He took the local bus to the next village and asked at a café how people were travelling while the line was closed. The owner showed him a marked walking route that followed the river without crossing the damaged slope. It was longer than the railway journey, and he did not assume that a line on his phone was sufficient guidance: he bought a paper map from the shop beside the café. Having called his accommodation, he learnt that the owner could hold his room even if he arrived after dark. That gave him time to leave his heavy camera case in a secure locker at the bus station and carry only a smaller camera on the walk.

The detour took most of the afternoon. A bridge that had seemed an unremarkable mark on the map turned out to be built from two different sorts of stone, evidence of a repair Arun had never read about. He stopped to photograph it, then reached the village shortly before dusk. The next morning, the railway was still shut. Rather than wait at the station for an announcement, he explored on foot and spoke to a local guide about the other bridges. He returned by bus two days later. The journey no longer resembled the one he had booked, but its unexpected route had given him the question that shaped the rest of his photographs: which changes to a bridge are meant to be seen?

title: The Voice in the Recording
passage:
For a school radio project, Jonah and his friend Farah interviewed residents about the old market. Farah asked the questions; Jonah edited the recording. The final programme sounded smooth, but Farah barely spoke to him after it was played. He assumed she was annoyed because he had shortened the interview with her grandfather. When he listened to the unedited files again, he realised that the more serious problem was elsewhere. He had kept Farah's questions but cut the moment when she explained why the market mattered to her family. Listeners had heard her voice without hearing her point of view.

Jonah's first impulse was to justify the cut by saying that the programme had a strict time limit. He stopped himself and asked Farah to listen with him to both versions. She pointed to a second omission: he had introduced the programme as though the interview plan were entirely his. She did not want the whole project withdrawn. The residents had given their time, and the broadcast was already available. What she wanted was an accurate account of the work they had done together.

Jonah apologised for making the edit without discussing it and told their teacher exactly which parts of Farah's contribution had been lost. With her agreement, he prepared a revised online recording that restored a shorter version of her explanation and corrected the introduction to name them both. The broadcast itself could not be replayed, so he did not pretend that a revised file erased the original mistake. For their next interview, they agreed to review the cuts together before either of them called a recording finished. Farah was still disappointed for several days, but she began sending him possible questions again. Their friendship recovered through a sequence of rather ordinary conversations, not through one perfect apology.

title: The Part They Did Not Get
passage:
Mira and Imani had rehearsed for the youth orchestra audition for months. They knew that only one of them could take the solo part, yet they had promised to keep practising together whatever happened. Imani was chosen. At the results board, someone asked Mira whether she minded, and Mira replied that Imani had been given the part because the conductor already knew her family. She meant it as a bitter comment on her own disappointment. Imani heard it as a claim that her playing had not earned her place.

For a week, their conversations shrank to arrangements about rehearsal times. Mira considered telling their friends that the remark had merely been a joke, but that would have repeated the suggestion in a different form. Instead, she asked Imani whether they could speak after practice and listened while Imani described what the comment had cost her. Several younger players now repeated it whenever she made a mistake. Mira apologised without asking Imani to reassure her, and told the players who had heard the remark that it was unfair and unfounded.

Their friendship did not immediately return to its old shape. Imani said she needed time, and Mira respected that rather than recruiting the conductor to settle the matter for them. At the next rehearsal Mira still turned up to play her own orchestral part; she did not stop making music because she had missed out on the solo. When Imani asked for help with a difficult passage a fortnight later, Mira offered to practise the rhythm with her, though she avoided taking over the interpretation. They eventually talked about the audition again, this time including Mira's disappointment and Imani's exhaustion. Neither needed to pretend the result had been easy. Being able to speak honestly about it was what allowed them to play together once more.
topic: How Mira tried to repair her friendship with Imani

option3: Asked the conductor to decide how the two friends should make peace.

title: A Watch for the Open Sea
passage:
For centuries, sailors could work out how far north or south they were with considerably more confidence than how far east or west. Longitude required a reference point: if a navigator knew the time at a fixed place and compared it with local time at sea, the difference would reveal a ship's east–west position. Keeping that reference time on a moving, damp vessel was the difficult part. In 1714, the British Parliament offered a substantial reward for a workable way to find longitude at sea.

John Harrison, a carpenter who had taught himself clockmaking, first produced sizeable marine clocks. His fourth design, completed in 1759, was strikingly different. H4 resembled an unusually large watch rather than a pendulum clock, and its design emerged partly from a smaller watch made to Harrison's specifications. Its ability to keep time at sea was tested on voyages, including a trial connected with Barbados. The results met the demanding accuracy standard set by the Longitude Act. An accurate instrument, however, was not automatically a practical device for an entire fleet.

The commissioners wanted Harrison to explain the principles of H4 and to demonstrate that other makers could reproduce its performance. They recommended a payment in stages, with the remainder dependent on that further proof. Harrison regarded this as a change to the terms under which he had worked, and disagreement about the reward continued. Testing also continued at Greenwich, where later results became another point of dispute. It would therefore be misleading to say that one successful voyage settled every question or immediately delivered the entire advertised prize.

H4 did help establish that accurate timekeeping could solve the navigation problem. Early marine timekeepers were costly, so widespread use depended on later makers finding ways to simplify and produce them more cheaply. The history of the instrument includes both an ingenious technical achievement and a prolonged argument about what counted as proof.
topic: Features of H4 and the official response to it
option1: Took the form of a large watch rather than another substantial sea clock.
option2: Relied on a swinging pendulum like a household clock.
option3: Met the accuracy requirement during its sea trials.
option4: Prompted a demand to show that other watchmakers could copy its performance.
option5: Brought Harrison the whole advertised reward as soon as the voyage ended.
option6: Was exempted from further testing after the Barbados trial.

Evidence: “H4 resembled an unusually large watch rather than a pendulum clock”

Evidence: “The results met the demanding accuracy standard”

Evidence: “demonstrate that other makers could reproduce its performance”

The passage instead says: “rather than a pendulum clock”

title: Reading the Stone
passage:
When soldiers found the Rosetta Stone in Egypt in 1799, its importance lay in a fairly ordinary administrative fact: the same decree appeared in three scripts. One was ancient Greek, which scholars could read; the others were Egyptian hieroglyphs and demotic, a more cursive Egyptian script. The stone did not contain a tidy alphabet with one symbol conveniently labelled by another. Much of it was damaged, and the relationship between the scripts demanded careful comparison. Copies and impressions were therefore distributed to scholars in Europe, allowing work to proceed beyond the place where the object was kept.

Thomas Young began by dividing the Greek text into sections and looking for corresponding groups in the unfamiliar writing. He compared recurring words with recurring signs, treating repetition as a clue rather than guessing from the pictures alone. Such comparisons revealed something useful, although the number of hieroglyphic signs made a simple one-sign-per-letter solution unlikely. He also made important progress with demotic. His work did not supply an instant translation of every Egyptian inscription; it helped establish a way to ask more precise questions.

Jean-François Champollion approached the problem with a different range of languages. He studied Coptic, a later form of Egyptian, because it might preserve words and sounds from the older language. That route included errors: at one stage he mistook a papyrus written in hieratic for a specimen of demotic and had to revise his assumption. He continued to compare names and inscriptions, eventually recognising that hieroglyphs could represent sounds as well as carry other kinds of meaning. The familiar pictures were part of a writing system capable of recording speech, not merely a gallery of objects and ideas.

The breakthrough is often attached to a single name, but the work depended on shared copies, earlier attempts and corrections to mistaken theories. Even after the central insight, scholars continued refining their reading of ancient Egyptian texts. The stone opened a route into a language; it did not make every text transparent at once.
topic: Methods scholars used to investigate Egyptian writing
option1: Insisted that every picture stood only for the object it showed.
option2: Matched recurring Greek words with repeated groups in other scripts.
option3: Avoided working from copies until they could inspect the stone in Egypt.
option4: Studied a later Egyptian language for clues to older words and sounds.
option5: Treated a damaged text as a complete alphabet with labelled letters.
option6: Recognised that some hieroglyphs could convey spoken sounds.
explanation:
Correct notes

2. Matched recurring Greek words with repeated groups in other scripts.
Evidence: “He compared recurring words with recurring signs”

4. Studied a later Egyptian language for clues to older words and sounds.
Evidence: “He studied Coptic, a later form of Egyptian, because it might preserve words and sounds”

6. Recognised that some hieroglyphs could convey spoken sounds.
Evidence: “hieroglyphs could represent sounds as well as carry other kinds of meaning”

Why the other notes do not fit

1. Insisted that every picture stood only for the object it showed.
The passage instead says: “hieroglyphs could represent sounds as well as carry other kinds of meaning”

3. Avoided working from copies until they could inspect the stone in Egypt.

title: What Remained After the Fair
passage:
Visitors to London's Great Exhibition of 1851 entered a temporary glass and iron building in Hyde Park that soon acquired the name Crystal Palace. Its size was impressive, but the difficulty for the organisers was intellectual as well as architectural. More than 100,000 objects were displayed. To keep the collection navigable, the exhibits were divided into broad groups: raw materials, machinery, manufactured goods and fine art. This arrangement suggested a journey from materials through making to decoration, although a visitor could still wander in an entirely different order.

The floor plan also reflected the politics and commerce of the period. Britain and territories of its empire occupied the western side; other participating nations shared space on the eastern side, allocated in relation to their trade with Britain. It was an international exhibition, but the spaces were not distributed equally. Over the following months more than six million people visited. The crowd came for an extraordinary range of things, from industrial machines to objects made by craftspeople. Calling it a simple celebration of inventions misses both the variety of the displays and the questions of representation behind them.

Once the exhibition closed, the organisers faced another decision: whether its effects should end with the dismantling of the temporary venue. They had made a surplus. Under Prince Albert's guidance, the commissioners used profits to buy land in South Kensington for cultural and educational institutions. A selection of exhibited objects was also acquired to help form a new museum of manufactures, an early stage in the history of today's Victoria and Albert Museum. The display itself did not remain in Hyde Park as a permanent museum, and its objects were not simply thrown away.

The legacy can thus be traced in buildings, collections and ideas about public education. The exhibition made enormous claims about progress, but it also left the practical question of who had space to show their work and who would benefit from the institutions built afterwards.
topic: The arrangement and later legacy of the Great Exhibition
option1: Grouped displays by the kinds of materials and work they represented.
option2: Allocated identical floor space to every participating nation.
option3: Placed Britain and its empire in a different section from other nations.
option4: Kept the Crystal Palace in Hyde Park as the permanent museum.
option5: Disposed of every exhibited object after the fair closed.
option6: Used proceeds to establish educational institutions in South Kensington.

title: The Stones That Travel Slowly
passage:
Across the level, dry floor of Racetrack Playa in California's Death Valley, stones sit at the ends of long tracks in the mud. Some tracks run almost parallel, suggesting that several stones moved at once, although no ordinary visitor is likely to catch them doing it. A rock can remain still for years. The traces inspired explanations involving fierce winds, slippery mud and even people secretly dragging the stones. The difficulty was that a track showed the result, not the conditions under which it formed.

Researchers eventually observed movement after setting up instruments and cameras. The playa had first filled with enough water to form a shallow pool around the rocks. During a cold night, a thin sheet of ice formed on its surface. When the sun warmed the pool, the sheet broke into floating panels. A light wind then pushed those panels against the exposed rocks, and the rocks slid over soft mud beneath the water. The ice did not have to lift the stones clear of the ground, nor did the wind have to reach the strength of a storm. In fact, the observed ice was too thin to grip large rocks in the way some earlier theories required.

The movement was slow enough to be almost invisible without a fixed point for comparison. This helps explain why someone standing nearby might have missed it. Several conditions also have to coincide: a pool of suitable depth, a freezing night, a warming day and wind at the right moment. Desert heat is part of the setting, but cold weather makes this particular event possible. The stones can leave their tracks during a brief, unusual interval; afterwards the water disappears and the surface again resembles a dry, motionless lakebed.

The explanation is more interesting than a single powerful force. A series of modest changes to water and ice can move rocks that would otherwise seem impossible to shift.
topic: Conditions and forces involved in the stones’ movement
option1: A steep slope makes the stones roll downhill.
option2: A shallow pool forms around stones before they move.
option3: Storm-force winds drag the rocks across bare, dry ground.
option4: Floating ice panels press against the rocks as they drift.
option5: Gentle wind can help push the ice that moves the stones.
option6: A thick ice sheet lifts large stones completely off the mud.

Evidence: “filled with enough water to form a shallow pool around the rocks”

Evidence: “the sheet broke into floating panels. A light wind then pushed those panels against the exposed rocks”

5. Gentle wind can help push the ice that moves the stones.
Evidence: “A light wind then pushed those panels against the exposed rocks”

title: When the Ground Becomes Sky
passage:
Photographs of Bolivia's Salar de Uyuni can look as if people are walking through clouds. In the rainy season a shallow covering of water reflects the sky so precisely that the horizon can nearly disappear. It is tempting to imagine a permanent lake, yet for much of the year the surface is dry and white. It is a salt flat, an immense crust largely made of minerals such as halite, the substance we know as common salt. Its changing appearance depends on the seasons, not on a switch between two different places.

To understand the salt, it helps to picture the plateau's older geography. Large lakes once occupied parts of the Altiplano. As their waters shrank, minerals became concentrated. The region is a closed basin: water flowing in has no route out to the ocean. During dry periods, evaporation left salts behind, gradually building the flat crust. Later rains can spread across its exceptionally level surface, producing the temporary mirror that draws photographers. An unusually wet season may extend that mirror much farther, but the water does not cover the whole salar throughout the year.

The surface has another audience beyond tourists. Its breadth, stability and strong reflectance make it useful to researchers checking measurements from satellite instruments. From orbit, an expanse that changes between bright salt and standing water offers a view of seasonal conditions across the high plateau. On the ground, however, an unusually extensive flood can interrupt travel across the flat. The fact that the landscape is level does not guarantee a safe route in every season.

Salar de Uyuni therefore holds two kinds of record. The salt preserves evidence of lakes that have disappeared over thousands of years, while each rainy season leaves a much shorter-lived image of the present sky. The mirror is remarkable precisely because it is temporary.
topic: Physical features that shape Salar de Uyuni
option1: Occupies a basin whose water has no outlet to the sea.
option2: Is covered by a deep permanent lake in every season.
option3: Has a dry mineral crust for much of the year.
option4: Owes its white surface chiefly to volcanic ash.
option5: Develops a reflective layer of water during the rains.
option6: Has a steep, uneven surface that prevents water from spreading.

title: A Forest of Stone
passage:
On the western side of Madagascar, the landscape of Tsingy de Bemaraha is sometimes described as a forest made of stone. The comparison is useful from a distance: innumerable grey pinnacles rise above patches of green. Up close, however, the surface is far from an orderly stand of columns. Sharp limestone ridges are separated by deep cuts and narrow passages, and the Manambolo River runs through a striking gorge. A visitor looking for a broad, uninterrupted plateau would be surprised by how thoroughly the rock has been divided.

The stone has a longer history than the plants around it. Limestone formed from an ancient seabed became a raised plateau, and water gradually wore away softer parts and sharpened the remaining rock. The dramatic shapes were formed through erosion of limestone, rather than from cooling streams of volcanic lava. The same complicated relief helps create varied habitats: forest grows around and below some of the pinnacles, while nearby lakes and other protected habitats support rare species. The stone is the most memorable image, but it is only one part of the place's ecological significance.

Protection of the region has also changed over time. Tsingy de Bemaraha was listed as a World Heritage site in 1990. In 2023, the recognised property was extended to include several additional protected areas and given the name Andrefana Dry Forests. The original reserve remains a component of that wider collection of parks and reserves. Its inclusion is based on remarkable natural scenery and biodiversity, not on a collection of historic buildings constructed among the peaks.

There is a tension in the phrase ‘forest of stone’. It captures the first impression while concealing the actual forests that grow alongside the limestone. Reading the landscape requires both views: the long geological processes that carved its ridges, and the living communities that occupy the spaces between them.

option2: Has limestone pinnacles separated by narrow passages and cuts.
option3: Forms one component of a larger protected World Heritage property.
option4: Is a smooth, unbroken plateau without a river gorge.
option5: Includes forest and other habitats that support rare species.
option6: Received recognition primarily for buildings constructed among the peaks.
